utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in the courtroom and those assisting us just outside the courtroom. I'm informed, Mr. Stamp, that you'd like to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, first I have to ask the registrar to call the case, because otherwise your words might be lost.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Not only for calling the case, but also for reminding me that had to be done. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May it please you, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I just raise two issues briefly. The Prosecution has received from the Defence its letter dated the 24th of January, 2003. And subsequently, a letter dated the 26th of January, 2003. The letter of the 24th of January sets out the order of the witnesses ending with the witness Sinisa Krsman on Friday, the 31st of January, 2003. Apparently that is the last fact witness. And the letter of the 26th of January continues with the witnesses, these now being the experts, and sets out the order of the expert witnesses beginning with Professor Dr. Kosta Cavoski, I think, on the 3rd of February, 2003. This issue really is a question which we seek to raise through the Court, and it is whether or not the Prosecution should interpret this order of witnesses to mean that the accused will not be called to testify, and this question is raised in light of the oral order of the Court on the 22nd of January that he should be made available to testify before proceeding with the evidence of the experts. That is the first issue which we would seek some clarification of. The next issue arises only in respect of the letter of the 26th of January in which the Defence has allocated or proposed certain time periods for the examination-in-chief of the expert witnesses. Normally, the examination-in-chief of expert witnesses is a formality to just introduce the expert and his report, except if the report is not admitted into evidence, and the expert really is put up for cross-examination. There is, it is submitted, excessive time proposed in respect to these experts, particularly in respect to Dr. Janko Vilicic, for whom seven hours in chief has been proposed, the real danger being that new matters outside of any report prepared for which the Prosecution would not be able to adequately prepare might be raised in these circumstances. Those, may it please, Mr. President, Your Honours, are the matters I'd like to bring to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps we first deal with the first part. You asked how to interpret --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First question was on how to interpret the, if I may say so, the procedural behaviour of the Defence. Perhaps the best way of finding out is just to ask the Defence. I take it the Defence is aware of the interpretive problems the Prosecution has raised. Perhaps we deal first with that matter, and then go into the time allocated for experts. Ms. Pilipovic or Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is there --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's always difficult to know how to interpret things, but I think General Galic's position is clear, and he rephrased it here. With all due respect, as the matter stands, he cannot take a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Defence, therefore, says that it will not indicate whether General Galic will be called as a witness. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we should add that if we don't call him, it's because we won't be able to, not because of a lack of will on our part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the Chamber has made it quite clear that if you would keep open the opportunity to call General Galic as a witness, you should provide the information necessary for the Prosecution to prepare for cross-examination. At the same time, the Chamber has clearly indicated that if finally you would decide not to call General Galic as a witness, that you could say that up to the last moment. I think it's a matter of practical -- it's a practical matter that you give some indication as whether you want to keep that opportunity open and reserve time for that. If the Defence still intends to call General Galic with, as the Chamber has decided before, the right up to the last moment to decide not to call him, it should be clear that it does. Therefore, you provided some information for the Prosecution to prepare for cross-examination which suggests that you want to keep open the opportunity to call General Galic as a witness. The Chamber also has instructed the Defence, since the order of appearance of witnesses is under the control of the Chamber, that if General Galic would be called, it should be done before expert witnesses are heard. And I do understand the Prosecution to raise the issue that not reserving time on the one hand side, and at the same time providing material for the preparation of cross-examination, seems to be a bit contradictory. So therefore, I would like to know, at least I think the Prosecution is entitled to know, how to interpret what seems to be a contradiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. You're quite right, when you say "what seems to be a contradiction" because when we examine the case in its entirety, and we are told that we have formed a request with regard to this decision, the things remain as they are. For the 23rd, we asked for permission from your Chamber to appeal against this

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: or not, once we have heard the testimony of expert witnesses, this is our position. So I don't think we're playing a game of cat and mouse. We are very clear. We think that the testimony, if it should be given, should be given under certain conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, may I ask for a redaction of page 4, lines 19 and 20. Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you read it, you know what is the confidential part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise. I'm very sorry. Thank you. Thank you Judge Nieto-Navia for having seen the problem. Our position is clear. As long as we don't know how things are as far as these elements are concerned then the position is delicate, so it doesn't seem useful for us, if we say at the end, that given the procedure, we accept and we only -- we don't think the hearing can be held. This will have to do with the decisions that the Defence will take with regard to the procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The issue is not raised just simply as a procedural matter which should be ironed out. There are enormous practical considerations for the Prosecution in respect of this. We would expect that if the accused is to testify soon or next week, that we would be in possession of a list of exhibits and a proposed time that the testimony will take in chief. And it is exceedingly difficult to do anything without those practical considerations being taken care of.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if I can add something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've tried to respect your order as much as possible especially with regard to the information. We've provided information about the possible contents, which seems extremely detailed. It didn't just mention shelling and sniping. We provided an entire list of very detailed questions, and I think that the Prosecution is perfectly capable of starting its work if it thinks it's necessary and useful. All the more so, in that it knows that these documents are ones that it is aware of in general. So it's not as if the Prosecution is totally ignorant and would be surprised by the timetable. The Prosecution has the time to prepare itself, the documents themselves are not of a central importance at this moment in time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider the matter over the first break, and then we'll come back to it. The second issue, the time to be spent on the examination-in-chief of expert witnesses, I think that a decision has been filed yesterday in which the Chamber has, in respect of certain expert witnesses, granted less time than requested and left it open for other expert witnesses. I think especially the background witnesses, I think altogether for three witnesses, a total amount of three hours was granted to be allocated as the Defence seems fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is the reason for which I don't understand the Defence's attitude, simply because it ignores the existence of the decision I have in front of me, now things are more clear to me. We are talking about something that has already been decided. With regard to this matter, Mr. President, if the Defence should appeal against your decision, I would be glad if we could get a decision very rapidly, because we think that it is necessary to have more time than the three hours which should be used for all the witnesses concerned. Naturally, this is for practical reasons. For practical reasons, we ought to know about this quite soon because I think that the end of the case is approaching. And in the case of Dr. Radovan Radinovic, we need to have information as soon as possible because if we had to ask for more, I don't see how in practical terms we would be in a position to make this function. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Take as a guideline, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that where expert witnesses have expressed themselves in long statements that could be easily read without further explanation, that there's less time needed to examine these expert witnesses in chief. For example, the Prosecution has taken only very little time to examine in chief Mr. Donia. But I see that you're asking us that if the Defence should appeal against your decision, I would be glad if we could get a decision very rapidly. It's not quite clear to me what decision exactly you're asking for here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. I didn't -- see in the transcript. I said if we had to request an appeal against your decision that we are discussing at the moment, dated the 27th of January, 2003, in that case, we would be grateful if the case should be -- could be treated quite rapidly. Yesterday, you stated that no one was perfect. This is the case for the Defence. I can confirm that because for some of these expert reports, there are certain mathematic formulas which consist of four or five lines. But if we manage to understand them, I would congratulate you. But the Defence can't understand them. And it will be necessary to explain this at length. We have never had a situation before. Introducing mathematics or physics in this case is something that requires time in order for these matters to be explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's exactly the reason why you'll find not yet a time limit on the experts in respect of mathematics. I think it's not the first time we hear such evidence but the mathematics become more and more complicated. The Chamber is aware of that, and that needs time. How much exactly also depends on how we proceed. But there are no clear time limits set for these, I would say, forensic scientists. So therefore, I don't know -- still, it's not clear to me what kind of decision you're expecting here. As I said, that the Chamber has not said it was not at the outset the issue. The issue was admissibility rather than the time, but we included the decision on the time to be spent in examination-in-chief, but not on the forensic scientist.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but we're speaking about the expert Radinovic. We're going to re-examine your decision. But what we would like, Mr. President, there are two possibilities: Either your Chamber will reconsider its decision, maybe it has already done so, and then will grant us more hours. Or your Chamber will authorise an immediate appeal or won't. If it did authorise such an immediate appeal, we would like your decision to be made as soon as possible so that if the experts come, the expert reports don't have to be divided, cut up, because there's nothing worse than having bits and pieces of testimony when we're dealing with expert witnesses. We would like to be in a position to follow the line of reasoning of these expert witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. You are drawing your attention to two possible developments, the first one being that we reconsider our decision; the second one, that we grant an immediate appeal. There is a third possibility that we do not reconsider our position and we would not grant a certificate. So we will let you know as soon as possible which of the three scenarios will be the one followed by this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We should say that we're going to re-examine your decision, and we will very briefly give you a brief summary of the reasons for which we think that this is not sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll come back to the matter in due course. Then, is the Defence ready to resume examination. I think I said yesterday there was approximately one-half hour left. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bukva. May I remind you you are still bound by the solemn declaration you had given at the beginning of your testimony. Examination-in-chief will now be resumed. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could we very rapidly, with the assistance of the usher, could we place the two documents that we are interested in on your table. And could you very quickly tell us whether you recognise this type of document, and do the contents seem to be correct to you? But do so very briefly. I think the numbers concerned are 936 and 1025, but this should be verified because I no longer have these documents in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It's a document dated the 6th of August, 1993. That's Document 936. The allegations in item 1 are correct, The action of the enemy with an 82-millimetre mortar directed at the Kula area. Kula is a prison, civilian prison. And on that occasion, one mortar shell fell on the grounds of the prison while the prisoners were walking around in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to interrupt you because we're running out of time. Can you just confirm whether according to what you can remember, this is correct, and then we'll move on to other matters.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's have a look at the other document, please. Could you read out the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's dated the 3rd of September, 1993. And it is number D1035.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recognise this type of document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you have a look at the same items we are interested in, the ones that have to do with hostile activity, and tell us whether as far as you can remember the information is correct or not.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of the 1st Romanija-- yes, that's correct. On that day in my diary, it says that the Muslims again tried to cut off the Pale/Lukavica Road.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. But as far as you can remember, is this correct or not? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the assistance of the usher, [In English]... To distribute that. We'll provide you with Document Number 864. Could you please have a look at it as in the previous cases. And then 748.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this type of document? Very well. As far as you can remember, the contents are correct? Witness, could you speak out aloud. Witness?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Please, take your time.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that there was action from the Hladnjaca direction because at the time, that was the end of June, I was in Rajlovac Brigade. And this has to do with action taken against its positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Which document do you have in front of you, please?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Document 864 dated the 22nd of July, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. And a minute ago, which document were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A minute ago it was 748.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. So you have confirmed these two documents? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Characteristic event that was recorded for the first time was the use of certain cluster bombs. I remember that very well. And this is mentioned. So this event is an event that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. With the assistance of the usher, another document, 861. It's dated the 17th of July, 1994. And we'll provide you with Document 748 dated 19th of June, 1994. And once more, Witness, on each occasion tell us whether you can recognise the type of document and then we'll be interested in item 1 and your confirmation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could it just be indicated --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the fighting that is indicated. I cannot do it. I have to ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. You asked about Document 861, yes, and you're rushing through at such a speed that the usher and registrar were not even able to provide 861. If you would have provided it just prior, before the start of the hearing of today, it would have been no problem. But you can't put five questions. I also wonder how much time the witness has to read what he seems to confirm. So I do understand your time problems, but at the same time, we should not rush in such a way that it becomes incomprehensible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, with pleasure. Thank you, Mr. President. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you have before you two documents. Let us take them in order. First, 741. And for the 741, I have two questions. They are always the same questions. First of all, do you recognise this type of the document? And secondly, the authenticity of item 1.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is consistent with the usual form of this type of document. And events from item 1 are of such nature that I cannot remember them with certainty because these were usual events, nothing specific, characteristic, reminds me, takes me back to these events except for the sniping activity in the area of the Vrbanja mosque, which is the Ljubljanska Street. I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. The following document, 861.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Document 861 dated 17th of July, 1994, is consistent with the form. Enemy activity on the area of responsibility of the 1st Sarajevo Motorised Brigade in the area of the Jewish cemetery is characteristic. And I think that this was in relation to one of the attempts to cut off the road between Sarajevo, Lukavica/Pale. So there was activity in the defence area of the Jewish cemetery. That is, there was firing in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the assistance of Mr. Usher, we will need his assistance on another two occasions. Here are two documents, if you can please distribute them with the same proviso.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And Witness, can you please start with the document bearing the number of 735, please, followed by Document 1111. First document, 13th of June, 1994, Document Number 735. Witness, what can you tell us about its type?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is authentic, and the events in the area of responsibility of the Ilidza Brigade, when the enemy forces fired on the Caritas convoy in the Cekrcici area is true. And the rest of item 1 is in relation to engineer fortifications done by the enemy of their positions. And what was in force, there was a cease-fire in force, and their activity was in a position to the cease-fire, so this is all true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, the same question for Document 1111, that is the document dated 7th of October, 1993, about its form. What can you tell us about its type?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is authentic. In item 1, there is talk of activity in the area of Mojmilo hill. For the most part, this time there was an attack on Muslim forces in the area of Djukica Potok which is mentioned here, and all the other operations were to do with this attack. The firing on Grbavica with the sniper from Debelo Brdo and so on. Everything was in relation to the activities previously mentioned. And this is a truthful event, this really happened, and it's all to do with the attack on Djukica Potok.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Usher -- Witness, with the assistance of Mr. Usher, could we please have the distribution of three documents this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And now, Witness, I'm going to ask you the same questions again. Document 543, in relation to 13th of March, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 13th of March, 1994, Document 543?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the document is authentic in any case. This date reminds me of intensive sniper activity carried out by the enemy in the direction of Novakovica Kuca. This event related here is true. And there was small-arms fire towards Novakovica Kuca and Kaponiri. That's what I can confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, can you please have a look at the document dated 7th of September, 1993 bearing the number 1.039.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is authentic, and the events reported here in paragraph number 2, and -- here we have talk that enemy opened fire throughout the day, sniping fire in the direction of Lukavica, and this is correct. This took place on the 7th of September, 1993. I recall that within the compound of the barracks near the command, a civilian was wounded on this date - I do recall that - from Muslim positions at Mojmilo hill. That day, there was an intense infantry attack on the position of the 1st Romanija Brigade, and I recall that according to the report that I received from my subordinate, this attack was very brief. In fact, it was an unsuccessful attempt without any serious consequence except one wounding.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, can you please keep that document. Thank you. And I have a following question: What about item 1? Do you confirm the item 1?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, where the witness referred to paragraph 2, did you not refer to the second linear of paragraph 1? The witness, as far as I understand, has only testified on the translated part. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Mr. President. I just wanted to make things clear so there's no confusion in the record. Now everything is crystal clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now, Witness, document dated 3rd of October, 1993. What can you tell us about the type of the document and the contents of item 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we clarify this date, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that we're looking at Document 1108.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is a problem with the date. It's not the 3rd of October. It is the 4th of October, and the number that I gave was 1108. Perhaps I'm going too fast. I'm going to slow down a little since everyone has been asking me to slow down. I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Same question, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is authentic. And the content in item 1 is fully authentic. This is one of the more peaceful days which was occasionally interrupted by sniping activity from enemy positions on Mojmilo hill on our positions in Lukavica. I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You can set them aside, these two documents. And with the assistance of Mr. Usher, these documents can be handed back. I will leave this aspect now. As far as the documents are concerned, I'm going to ask you some general questions, and these general questions are to do with instructions. Witness, what can you tell us, very briefly, regarding the humanitarian-related instructions that were transmitted to you or not transmitted by the military hierarchy, military chain of command, towards the troops? Clearly, were there any instructions, any orders to the troops, in relation to the respect of civilians in times of combat, and if there were any instructions, can you tell us what they were?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, I'm a professional soldier, and I am well aware of the principles and provisions of the Geneva Conventions in relation to the respect of the laws of war. And I am aware that the command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps worked on this plan that the main elements of the aforementioned conventions be taught, instructed, to the front-line soldiers. I had an occasion to stop by a trench on Trebevic next to the road. And in that very same trench, I saw some excerpts from the Geneva Conventions that regulate the matters. So I can responsibly claim that the troops, even soldiers, were aware of them, knew them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We're going to go on to another subject --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I noticed that elements of your question just put to the witness were not translated because you included the necessity of such instructions when asking the question to the witness, so it was not as neutral as it is written in the English language. I remember you saying "necessaire, instruction necessaire." Perhaps just for the transcript, and since the Prosecution will not have understood it if they listen to the English translation and when they looked at the English transcript, that it is clear, at least, what the question exactly was. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Indeed, I wasn't keeping an eye on the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, we're going to change the subject, and we are going to look at the aspect of respecting of Conventions. That is, the aspect of provisions for punishment if such Conventions were not respected. As far as this is concerned, does the name of an officer called Mr. Dunjic, does this name say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us, tell the Chamber, what happened in the Dunjic case, very briefly, please, if you know this, of course.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know everything in relation to this case. Dunjic was the commander of the Igman Infantry Brigade, and very frequently, if you can say that, which is -- I mean, frequently being a relative term -- he behaved, one could say, as a paramilitary in a sense that he behaved in a superficial, inappropriate manner, and he did not fully follow the orders of the superior. He behaved in an appropriate way of his own will and was not fulfilling the standards of subordination. That is the reason why my commander replaced this brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you say "my commander," who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Galic, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We are still within the same subject, but do you know any other examples that may have happened to some officers or perhaps soldiers of inferior rank? Or, for instance, that brigade commanders may have taken decisions in relation to platoon commanders or company commanders? Do you know of any such examples? If you do not recall at this moment, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't recall that. These problems that were successfully handled by brigade commanders at their level, and most of the time, they didn't come to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We are going to another question. Witness, were you in Sarajevo on the 24th of December, 1992, and then the 6th or the 7th or the 6th and the 7th January 1993? And I'm specifying this during the night, the night of the 24th and 25th December 1992 and the night of the 6th and the 7th January 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you ever heard that there was on one of these two dates, these two time periods, either during the Orthodox Christmas or during the Catholic/Protestant Christmas, formally speaking, that there was barrage fire which would have lasted for at least 20 minutes, and during which all weapons around Sarajevo would have opened fire on to the city?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. You stand by that, you're categoric in that answer?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm going to change the subject, but we don't have much time. So now, cultural monuments or facilities, have you ever seen an order during your service that would have been aimed at targeting any kind of cultural facility or monument in the area of Sarajevo remained under the control of the BH army? And when I mean "cultural" -- when I say "cultural," I mean museum, mosque, any important cultural document, historical monument, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have never seen such an order. And as far as I know, none of these facilities in the part of Sarajevo under Muslim control were ever hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you please tell us if destruction - and when I say "destruction," I don't mean occasional, but significant destruction that happened on the Serb side as well occurred?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can confirm, for instance, that following the liberation of Trnovo, we found the church, Orthodox church, in a ruinous state. It had been burned, it had no roof, et cetera. As far as other instances are concerned, I couldn't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we now please move on to specific things. Could you confirm -- no, I'm going to rephrase. Names: Jug, Operation Koverta mean anything to you, Koverat? K-O-V-E-R-A-T.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Operations Jug, Koverat 1, Koverat 2, knees were both Muslims offence both outside rings of Sarajevo, and they were both offensive with a view to lifting the blockade of Sarajevo. And I repeat, this is what these offences were called by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the intensity of these offensives?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They tried to prepare themselves well and prepare the offensives well, and in that sense they engaged a large number of troops. At this very moment specifically, I cannot recall, but in any case, these were much, much stronger forces than the Sarajevo Romanija Corps forces. I could -- although we don't have time, I could speak about one of the last offensives that when they attempted to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they attempted to break through in the area of Kokoska, it's an elevation point in the area of responsibility of the Igman Infantry Brigade. According to our data, during this offensive, some 8.000 troops took part because they had a significant number of people killed during this offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Does the name of St. George mean anything to you in terms of offensive?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a paramilitary unit that we demilitarised as part of an operation that we carried out with the objective of eliminating those kind of units.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us about any other troops or units that may have suffered the same fate, that the corps would have placed under its command or that they would have been eliminated, removed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this unit, this group, St. George, they ended up in prison because of murder of a Serbian person and because of the criminal offences on the ground. This is one of the more drastic examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can you tell us which criminal offences on the ground, apart from this murder?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is -- this was about systematic looting of property. Mostly they were stealing cars, of property generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you mean of both, so they were stealing property belonging to both ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, can we continue with the same line of questioning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, may I remind you that you are close to the time I indicated to you. As a matter of fact, you are there already. So would you please try to conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And may I just indicate for the record the last question was extremely leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll take note of both observations. I have been asked to slow down, I have done so. And I think that we could ask for a little additional time to conclude. We won't be much longer. I'll try and be as efficient as possible. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, with regard to the opposition which were intrinsic to the BH army --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'll repeat that. With regard to -- I'll rephrase this because I can see where the problem is. With regard to any possible problems of opposition that the BH army may have had within its structure, what can you tell us about such clashes, about such -- that should be translated by opposition, shock, clash, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, clashes within the BH army itself were quite frequent as far as we knew. My department was particularly interested in such events that occurred in the BH army. And in our opinion, we heard reliable information about all such conflicts. This happened very rapidly, or rather I mentioned Sarajevo criminals such as Juka, Celo Bajramovic, and then there was Caco, Musan Topalovic, Caco. When these local strongmen became stronger, became a serious threat, not just to the military hierarchy but also the political hierarchy, then the first conflicts within the BH army occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the Party of Democratic Action, those who were in power, but the Party of Democratic Action above all, attempted to eliminate such people. And it is a well-known fact that they killed Musa Topalovic, Caco.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did this conflict cause an exchange of fire between rival factions as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll rephrase then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: How far did this opposition go?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said in my previous answer, fire was opened, there was shooting in those conflicts as a result of those conflicts because Caco was killed. There were armed conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, Borsalino, Silos, Sunce, did these names mean anything to you? And if so, what do they mean? Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Everyone knows about these names, especially the Serbs who were imprisoned in those prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these notorious prisons in which Serbs were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any other places that you could mention?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an entire series of such prisons in Sarajevo according to our information. And it wasn't possible to verify this for certain. There were about 40 prisons, but it wasn't possible to verify all this information because there were private and even secret prisons.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the number of prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I want to ask you something us. You mentioned Maljutka yesterday. Could you tell us what a Maljutka is?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before we get to the Maljutka, could the witness just repeat the number of prisons he mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The interpreters have asked you to repeat that part of the answer. It means that how many prisons there were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to our information, about 40 prisons. I would just like to add, Hepok in the basement of that building on Malta. There was a prison in the basement of that building. There was the Viktor Bubanj barracks. That was a big prison for Serbs. And as I said, there are quite a lot of private prisons. It was difficult to record them all, but I think that up until the end of the war, there were some prisons which even the International Red Cross was not able to list, to record.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, with regard to the series of questions concerning cooperation, what can you tell us about international commissions or joint commissions that the army would have liked to establish in order to examine various issues, various problems, protests, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the event at Markale when the main staff ordered the formation of a mixed commission whose task would be to look into the circumstances of that event. I know that the commander drafted his own order on the basis of an order from his superior and appointed commission members on our side. And I know that that commission, or rather our members didn't participate in the work of that commission because UNPROFOR could not guarantee their safety, the safety of our people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, do you know whether there were any other examples of the desire to cooperate at the level of the establishment of these joint or common commissions?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I know that my commander encouraged any initiative taken in order to establish and reinforce a truce, or rather peace in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your commander, that is to say?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now answer two or three questions that have to do with Alipasino Polje, and we will come to a conclusion very soon. Do you know whether in the Alipasino Polje area, although you've already answered this with reference to the map, do you know whether in Alipasino Polje, in the area of Alipasino Polje, there was an target of any kind that your -- your intelligence service might have been interested in?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The leading element is already in. The witness was asked earlier to mark certain things on a map as far as I recall, and he did. Now contained in the question is a leading element, and the question could have been asked without leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. The leading element in the question is not such that the question is inadmissible. Please proceed. So the question, therefore, was whether there was any specific target of any kind that your service might have been interested in. I take it, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that you were asking whether there was any target in which the intelligence service was interested in. Yes. Could you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Alipasino Polje area, as far as I can remember -- I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Were there any factories in that area?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just for the record, although the leading element -- that again is leading to the extent of dragging. The witness said he can't recall, and now he has been pulled into something.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, to ask whether there were any factories, it's something I don't know, and I'm not leading if I ask the witness whether there were any factories there. The witness is free to say whether there was or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be some misunderstanding, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. The mere fact that the witness is free to answer whatever question does not exclude that the question is leading. On the other hand, it's clear that from its own recollection, the witness does not come up with anything that if there would be any specific interest for the Defence to know about factories, is there any special factory you would like to draw attention to in Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, now it's a matter of locating the part of town that has to do with Alipasino Polje. But perhaps the Zica factory is part of the Alipasino Polje zone, and there was a weapons and ammunition workshop there. We pointed it out on the map yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Witness, you mentioned the El Fatah group yesterday. Does the name Kulin Ban evoke anything?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was a brigade, a Croatian brigade. It was a brigade of the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council in the Kiseljak military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. We're approaching the end of your examination. I would like you to later on speak about the personality of General Galic. But first of all, the question has to do with a Maljutka. What is a Maljutka?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My military occupational specialty is that of a communications officer, but this has to do with an anti-armour device. Its designation is Polk 9K-11. It is an anti-armour missile which is launched and its purpose is to destroy armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you've already indicated what else you had to ask about. I said not more 10 minutes, it is now approximately 15 minutes, so you really have to conclude. So one or two questions, fine, but that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And just to be clear, one question and then the very last. Two questions, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My first question, Witness, what can you tell us about the -- in humanitarian terms, about the personality of General Galic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from the fact that he is an exceptional officer, I think that General Galic is a great humanist, a great humanitarian. Whenever the international forces would carry out humanitarian actions, whether it was the Red Cross or UNPROFOR, General Galic never obstructed such actions or put them into question. And on occasion, I think he even did far more than anyone else would have done. I would like to remind you that we are from Sarajevo and that after the Muslim powers let convoys of Slovenians and Jews and Macedonians and Romas pass through, and this was probably under the pressure of the international community, I have to remind you that not a single convoy of Serbs left Sarajevo. That I have to emphasise that I think that General Galic is a great humanitarian.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Since I only have one more question, I'm interested in the issue of crossing the runways at the Sarajevo airport before the famous tunnel was opened. My question is as follows: What can you tell us about the effective control that the BH army may have had over the two sides of the runway, on the Butmir side and on the Dobrinja side?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslim forces had total control over any movement over the runway. I mean, into the city and out of the city. And that's for the simple reason that they held positions there. And very often, we heard conversations through the channels of communications between local commanders from Butmir and Dobrinja. And from these conversations, it was quite clear that only soldiers were crossing the runway. That's quite clear, although after a political decision had been taken, we handed the airport over to UNPROFOR forces. In that document it said it can only be used for humanitarian reasons. But we have quite enough information to be able to claim that the airport runway was used for military purposes by the Muslims, mostly in order for the forces to regroup, to supply military equipment, ammunition, and other things that the forces in the town required.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. Mr. President, I have concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, is the Prosecution ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were shown some documents, purportedly combat reports from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps to the main staff. Am I understanding your evidence to be that these documents are consistent in form?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please rephrase the question. "Consistent," what do you mean by "consistent"?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said, I believe, that the form of the documents which you saw was consistent with the reports that were normally sent to the main staff.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the form of the documents is absolutely identical to the usual form these documents had.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And these documents referred to the enemy and events which you found were characteristic of the circumstances that you experienced while you were in Sarajevo at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, first of all --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks. Thanks. Could you have a look, with the assistance of usher, could you be shown Document 936. Do you see the first paragraph beginning with the number 1?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see the second paragraph just below that first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What's the first word of that second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "With a machine-gun..."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see the third paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is the first word of that third paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Turncoats".

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is that word a pejorative word or derogatory word for Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now we would have to discuss history in order to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's a simple question. Would any Bosnian Muslim you know consider that word being used to address him as derogatory or pejorative? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They probably would. The question is simple, but it's a little more complicated to give an answer. It would be necessary to examine history.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think the witness should be allowed to continue to the extent that this is possible. He had something to say and the Prosecution interrupted him. He could tell us why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I would invite Mr. Stamp perhaps to ask a short question about that. But I take it that Mr. Stamp is mainly interested in whether these type of expressions were used of which he asked the witness whether these are pejorative denominations, and not primarily what historic reason would explain the choice of exactly this term and whether there have been good reasons in the past. But -- and also, Mr. Stamp is allowed to use his time as he wishes. But Mr. Stamp, could you ask the witness to indicate very, very briefly where the word comes from so that the Chamber is also in a better position to understand what would be the meaning of "turncoats" in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell us in one sentence, two at the most, where the word comes from?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try and be brief. While the Bosnia and Herzegovina was under the Turks, part of the local inhabitants, and they were mostly Serbian and Croatian, converted to Islam. So the origin of the Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina is such. And this is why you can often hear this expression, "potorica" [phoen], which means turncoat or convert to Islam. It means someone who has changed his religion, who has converted to Islam.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. These reports refer in paragraph 1 in some detail, you'll agree with me, to activities by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do these reports refer in similar details to activity on these days by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you pay attention to item 2, it mentions the action taken by our forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And am I to understand from your answer that paragraph 2 is -- would be a detailed reference to the activities of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps on the relevant dates of these documents?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were there UNMOs and UNPROFOR personnel in some areas controlled by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and also within the city in the areas controlled by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were military observers there, but I don't know the exact number, nor do I know where they were positioned, where they were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you're guessing what is in my mind. We'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, we would like to start in private session. Could we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Defence has filed a request for a certificate for appeal on the decision of the Chamber in respect of the eventual testimony of the accused. The Chamber will not grant the certificate. A written decision will follow. Then I've got two very practical matters: Tomorrow, Wednesday, the Chamber is requested to sit in the afternoon rather than in the morning. As I understand, the parties have been informed that the Chamber intended to follow that request. And I was also informed that there were no objections that would not allow us to meet that request. So therefore, we'll sit tomorrow, Wednesday, in the afternoon, usual time, starting at a quarter past 2.00, same courtroom. Then for the 7th of February, where we were supposed to sit in the afternoon, a change of the court schedule is in preparation as well. I'd like to know from the parties whether there would a major problem if we would sit in the morning rather than in the afternoon of the 7th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have no problems with that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, before we give our answer, we have to know which day is that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 7th of February, I think it's a -- it's a Friday, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I accept, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the parties should -- it's not final yet, and especially it's not final yet at what time we would start in the morning. But it would be 9.00 or whether it would be 9.30 or even 9.45 or even 10.00. I take it from your nodding, General Galic, that when we discussed the 7th of February, there would be no major objections from your side as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's fine. If it was the 5th, then it wouldn't be good because I have physiotherapy. But it's the 7th, so it's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, General Galic. Then we could resume the cross-examination unless there are any questions from the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No questions, just a proposition if it would be acceptable to the Court. Having regard to the text of the examination-in-chief, there are some matters which arise which I would like to make inquiries into before the cross-examination is completed. I am told I will have some time over four hours. It would be much more economical in time and perhaps I might not even need to use that four hours if perhaps I could be allowed to go on tomorrow, if the cross-examination be broken up in two and another witness be taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time you think you would fill, so as to say, today? When would be the point that you would say whether or not to continue would depend on --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At the end of this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the end of this session. Of course, we first have to ask whether the -- apart from that, looking at the clock, you started cross-examining the witness at 20 minutes past 10.00. The Defence took four hours and 15 minutes in chief. So I take it that the Defence and the witness will be prepared to continue the cross-examination by tomorrow. Would the Defence be ready to call its next witness if the Prosecution would seek further inquiries so in order to -- not to waste any time, but to see whether they can examine as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you. First of all, as far as the practicalities are concerned, it seems that the Prosecution has lost an audiotape, and in order so that we can prepare, it would be good -- I understand that the case manager is on to it, so that we can have the original so that we can work this. And I understand the Prosecution is working with this. And the second point, Mr. President, we do not see why we would need to have a new rule which would authorise the Prosecution to cut up its cross-examination based on their needs. We are already, the Defence, and the Prosecution should be as well, to continue with the proceedings. Why can't the Prosecution just cross-examine, and we'll see what happens?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be possible that the inquiries you intend to make would result in taking less time in cross-examination than you would do without these inquiries?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed. Indeed, it probably would obviate the need to go into a variety of areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will consider the matter. Since you say it would be approximately the end of this session -- please indicate the moment where you would like to stop. And then the Chamber will consider the matter and take a decision on your request.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'd like to say the following: I believe that I will also have to examine in chief in part Major Indjic. Obviously, I'm following everything that's happening in the language which is not mine, and I am trying to focus as much as I can on a witness by witness basis, and I am trying to find my bearings among all the technical elements. If we are cutting things up in this way, this is adding another aspect and creating more problems. And I think that I'm not doing my job as being counsel in the Defence of General Galic. And I don't think that we need to complicate matters further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution ready to continue the cross-examination at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you then escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Piletta-Zanin, did you mention mnemo-technical elements?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you mention mnemo-technical elements?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, did I do that wrongly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Interpretation], no, but the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Has the transcript forgotten things?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was listening to French, so I wasn't looking at the transcript. [In English] Mr. Stamp, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you said that the paragraph 2 of these purported regular reports would give a detailed representation of the activities of the SRK on the relevant dates. Is it, therefore, possible that on any of these dates, the Serb -- the Sarajevo Romanija Corps could have fired off, say, 3.000 artillery rounds and it not be reported?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is it possible, for example, that the -- on any of these dates or any of these reports, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps could have fired artillery into Hrasnica to harass refugees and it not be reported?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. Harassing refugees in Hrasnica, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Hrasnica, there were no refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have a question which is referring to one of the dates, but -- no, I withdraw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I take it that by saying in Hrasnica, there were no refugees, you are saying that it is not possible for the SRK to have been firing rounds in an area in Hrasnica where there were refugees and it not be reported in these purported combat reports. Your answer is no?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. You cannot speak about opening artillery fire on refugees. That is not something we can talk about simply because this didn't happen. Artillery fire was open, if it was ever opened, exclusively on military targets and targets that were useful for such fire to be opened. And this fire was under complete control of brigade commanders. So if fire was opened, then in the report, the subordinate would have to say how he opened, with how many projectiles, and what the effect was of such fire that was opened. And any possibility can be ruled out that such fire was opened at refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Specifically, the reports which you were shown, all but one, purport to be regular combat reports of the SRK to the main staff of the VRS. Should those reports indicate how many artillery rounds were fired by the SRK and the effect of the use of artillery?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not necessary. It was enough to write, to include -- this is a daily, regular report. So it was enough just to put in what kind of activity was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. As an intelligence officer, were you aware -- withdrawn. As an intelligence officer, did it come to your attention that UNMO representatives were regularly prevented from carrying out their monitoring duties in some areas controlled by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not necessary for carrying out of my tasks, and I was never informed about this. It does not come within the remit of intelligence work. I'd just like to add that I personally believe that the military observers on the Serb side were accommodated in every sense so that they can get a realistic picture on the ground where they were deployed. And I know that the local commanders were given such instructions by the command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In September 1992, what rank were you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you were involved in intelligence gathering?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you remain an officer involved in intelligence gathering for Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 18437 to 18445. the next two years?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At any time did you -- were you posted to the Rajlovac Brigade in those two years?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You indicated that the accused had morning meetings with his staff. Were these daily morning meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these were daily meetings. And I have already described more or less their content and their purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said in the absence of your -- please look this way. You said in your absence, in the absence of your chief, you would attend some of these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you attended approximately 20 to 30 per cent of these meetings. I can't recall. Approximately how many of these meetings did you attend?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's more or less that. 25 to 30 per cent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So over a two-year period, you would have attended in excess of 100, 150 meetings with the accused?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not 30 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for instance, 80 to 90 meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And your responsibility would be to inform the accused and his staff as to important areas or important information that you received as a result of your duties?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not a daily responsibility, particularly at those kind of meetings. I think that you are well aware that intelligence service is a secret service. And all data gathered is gathered by the usual methods, well known, and with such information, such data, this is forwarded to the direct superior, to those within the service that need that information. So for anyone else outside of the service or were not superiors, it was not desirable for them to know the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Who was your commander, your direct commander?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps commander, that is General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When I say --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As part of that corps, and I think yesterday we elaborated, there was a section for intelligence and security matters. And this section was made up of two different departments. One was the department for intelligence matters, and I was the chief of that. And the second department was the security department. And the chief of the security department was also the chief of the intelligence and security section. Myself, as the chief of the intelligence department, speaking in terms of expertise, I was subordinate to the chief of the section for security and intelligence matters, and I was subordinated to the chief of staff, and I had to forward my information to him and also to the person who was my immediate superior. And that was the chief of the section for security and intelligence matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What's the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The chief of the section for security and intelligence matters.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, it was Colonel Lugonja.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At these regular meetings that you attended, would the accused receive reports as to the situation on the front lines?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained this, but I will repeat it now. The initial stage of the meeting, it was usual for the duty officer, operations officer, to report on the situation in the units based on the regular or interim combat reports that arrived to the operations centre of the corps command. In this way, the corps commander was informed and briefed on the situation on the ground and at the front line. So it was on the basis of the reports forwarded by -- compiled and forwarded by subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would the corps commander be informed about the use of ammunition, of heavy ammunition?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is one thing that has not been clarified fully, and it's related to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just, would the commander, the corps commander, be informed about the use of heavy ammunition?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, he would be. He would be informed for the simple reason that, and I have to clarify this point, that in regular or interim daily combat reports, it was important -- it was necessary to put factual situation because any false reporting would result in some sanctions that were very strict according to the rules that were valid in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there. I'm trying to ask questions that are pretty simple, and I ask for a simple reply. Can you just refrain, generally speaking, from the additional comments. If we need to ask more, we'll ask more. There is a time situation that we are trying to abide by. There were other meetings with the commander, I think you said, by specific departments of the corps. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: With certain organs of the corps command, and I said contrary to this, these were meetings of the corps command, core, C-O-R-E.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would there be meetings with the intelligence department and the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Subordination was such that the chief of the intelligence department in disciplinary, that is to say in military terms, was connected to the chief of staff. And it wasn't possible to bypass that level, and it wasn't necessary. So the direct link between the commander of the corps and the chief of the staff, well in such a case, we would have bypassed two levels. And military principles do not allow this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your department monitored the media in respect to the events that were occurring in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would you tell us what media was this? Or if more than one, could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For objective reasons, we were able to monitor the Muslim television and radio. There was no access to other media that was logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did the Muslim television and radio carry news items from other international media like CNN, BBC, Associated Press, of events that were happening in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To an extent, yes. Because the television and radio in a certain sense relayed BBC and CNN programmes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall saying that the Sarajevo Romanija Corps was taken advantage of in the media?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you say "taken advantage of," do you include reports in the media that members of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps shot at civilians or shelled civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The events in Sarajevo were commented on with bad intentions by the big media companies, the big international media companies. And it was clear to us that this sort of propaganda was planned. That's one of the reasons for which I occasionally monitored such media. We very often established that a certain event that had occurred in Sarajevo had absolutely nothing to do with the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. But the media carried news according to which this was the result of action taken by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, and this is how extensive propaganda was conducted against the SRK.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So therefore, I take it that you heard reports in the media that you monitored that the Sarajevo Romanija Corps shot at civilians and shelled civilians, but your position is that this was false?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's false, absolutely false. It's false to say that that happened. But I don't specifically remember seeing that in the media, but there was such information. But such events did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You indicated, am I right, that you thought it was your duty to monitor these reports or to monitor the media. Did you bring to the attention of the persons to whom you reported what the media was saying in respect to the SRK shelling or shooting at civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but you have obviously not under me correctly. A minute ago I said that I don't remember seeing such a report in the media. Secondly, it wasn't my duty to monitor the media. Yesterday, I said that that was one of the methods used to gather intelligence. However, information gathered in that way is not very reliable. And it's not possible to verify such information. And for this reason, they were not of great operational value. This was considered to be information the quality of which was not very high. But in order to avoid any confusion, I don't remember seeing something like that. You shouldn't think that all I did was watch television. This was something I did not do frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were the members of staff aware that there were reports in the media of the SRK shooting or shelling civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I can only speak about what I myself know. The question was whether I had seen anything like that in the media, and I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did the Sarajevo Romanija Corps have snipers? Do you know that? Were snipers used by the corps?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The formation of the SRK, after the assembly decision on forming the Army of Republika Srpska, this formation was carried out on the basis of the organisational rules that had been adopted from the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
