utterances.text: So did they have snipers? That's a simple question. Did they have snipers at all? Did they use them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any information about that. And I can claim quite categorically that I never saw this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you don't know whether or not the SRK had or employed snipers?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was it possible for the accused, General Galic, to contact and give orders to his field commanders immediately should he feel the need to do so? In other words, were there any means by which he could give immediate commands and receive information from commanders in the field?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President. The witness is not necessarily a telecommunications specialists or communications specialist. First of all, we should check to see what his technical competence is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I thought he said he was, but maybe I could ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please, if you would lay a foundation for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you trained in communications?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was the general capable of giving orders and receiving information from his commanders in the field should he so desire using means that would transmit the orders immediately or receive the information immediately?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The communications system, the way it was organised, was not something I was familiar with because I had other duties to perform, and I'm not able to answer that question. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You spoke about the airport. Were you aware of any protests made by UNPROFOR representatives to General Galic or his command staff in respect to the airport?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a fairly general question, and I don't know what you are thinking of specifically. But the question is a question that should be put to someone from the department for liaising with UNPROFOR. I personally was never in a position to see such a protest. So for me, there were no such protests. But please, be more specific. Which protest and with regard to what event at the airport?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Generally to shooting at persons crossing. You never heard of any protests from UNPROFOR in respect to that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We saw a video yesterday, and maybe I could use the opportunity to do something which I might have done earlier, to indicate -- to ask the technical personnel if they could get the video that was shown yesterday ready. There was what you said was a soldiers' club shown in that video. What is a soldiers' club?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a term that was used in the former JNA. It refers to the building which has facilities for entertaining soldiers. A cinema, a library, and I can't remember what else there was there. But this refers to a building that has such facilities, and it was called a soldiers' club. Various performances were organised there, plays on occasion, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did the General attend there from time to time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. Perhaps he went to the library.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will interrupt here. And now I am proceeding on a mnemo-technique basis. I think the French translation spoke about a club yesterday. I don't know if Mr. Stamp could be more specific. Is this what he's referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not entirely clear to me. Wasn't the nub of the question soldiers' club?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Mr. Piletta-Zanin said "riding club."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to determine what Mr. Stamp's question was, but I think that yesterday a riding club was mentioned. Matters are a little obscure to me now. Perhaps it's a matter of interpretation problems. We'll see. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't remember a riding club, but I'll find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it was in the French transcript which isn't on our screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He was talking about a soldiers' club and nothing else. That's what appears in the English transcript. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll look for that elsewhere. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With the leave of the Court, if the video is ready, could the video be played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the video be played, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This view as it goes now is taken from where?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered that question, but I'll repeat it. I'll repeat my answer. From one of the windows of the commander's office. Or it could also be from the window of my office, but it was from that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could the video be rewound just a bit. Could you go forward just a bit. I'm afraid I was on the wrong channel. Could you stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you tell us which area of Sarajevo is beyond those trees. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I've already said, part of Dobrinja is behind these trees. And then behind the central part of these trees, there is Donji Kotorac, Hrasnica, and Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you please proceed with the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Stop here, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have now moved on to a second part of the tape which is shot from a different place. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And now we see a white, two-storey building.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And it's the building that you said the accused's office was in as well as your office.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you proceed with the tape, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you stop here, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On the picture, can you see a yellow structure, a yellow-looking structure beside a house with a red top?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say what that structure is?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although the photograph is not very good, as far as I can remember, this is not a building. The yellow surface in this photograph is a -- is where a certain construction company keeps sand. What's it called? It's not a building. It's a silo, a sand silo. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you please proceed with the tape, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Could you freeze the image. Could you rewind a bit. There is one important detail which is very revealing. Could you just rewind it a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I wasn't asking about that. But -- stop there. Is that what you want?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Maybe a little earlier because as this car passes by this yellow part, you can see that there is a traffic sign. You can see that it's a traffic sign. I don't know if you can see that. It's a traffic sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Could we move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you stop there, please. Could you move forward or backward just a tad. Perhaps we could get a clearer picture. It's a little bit blurred. Very well. It's getting no better. Could you stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you make out a tall grey/white structure between the trees in the centre of this frame?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not very clear. But it's quite clear to me on the basis of the contours of this building that it's the Orthodox church in Veljine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where was this frame shot from? Can you say?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was shot from -- it was probably shot from the corner of the building where the commander and I had our offices. So it was from the corner of the building, the corner on which side the commander and I had offices and where we had windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This Orthodox church in Veljine, is that the one which overlooks Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The tape may be stopped now. Could the witness be shown Defence Exhibit 1858. That's a map. And I think we just want the left hand part of the map, the western section of the map. Could you move the map up a little bit more. Just a little bit more, please. The other direction, please. Should I put it this way. Could you move it so that more of the bottom section of the map is showing. A little bit more in that direction. Thank you. Could you leave it there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you make out where the church is on that map, the Orthodox church in Veljine? You can look on the map to your right if that is more convenient, if that is clearer.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's this building here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Using a blue pen, I think it is, could you just put a circle around that building. And that's a blue circle over the word "Dobrinja." Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the better understanding, Mr. Stamp, could you please ask the witness also whether you can see on this map the point from which the video was taken where you could see what the witness said was the Orthodox church.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps, Mr. Usher, you could help somewhat with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you see on the map the point from which the video was shot.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's this part here, this corner here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you -- you have put a dot there. Could you put something a little bit more bold, perhaps an X there.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom... Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sir, could we move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you put a new question to the witness, he might answer it, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The map could be taken back now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was your department involved in working with the corps artillery and mortar units in identifying targets?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't see how. There's no logic in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would you, if I could put it this way, assist the artillery units by giving them information as to where military targets were located?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is -- shows lack of understanding of military subordination. I thought I was precise. When the intelligence work of my service was mentioned, I remind you that all the intelligence information that I received I forwarded to the chief of staff. And from that moment on, I had no influence on what happened to that information whatsoever. I did my job with the objective of giving as much intelligence support as possible to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. But this data, information, was then used as it happened in the chain of command. But from that moment on, as I passed them on, I was no longer interested in the information. There was no possibility of communication, say, with the chief -- between the chief of the intelligence department and chiefs or heads of any artillery sections.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Am I to understand you to be saying that after you passed on information to the chief of staff, you did not become aware of how this information was used?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Am I to understand further from that that you were not aware of how the commanders or the method used by the commanders to distinguish between civilian and military targets when they were using information that you gave to them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question seems to me is quite complex. Could you perhaps simplify it, as there are several things that are unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you gave information with respect to possible targets, would you be aware of how or any method or means used by the commander or the persons to whom you gave information to distinguish civilians from military personnel?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to remind you that my service worked on gathering data on the enemy about its military formations, and we were exclusively interested in the enemy army, in the enemy troops. So -- which means that we were not working on gathering data related to civilians. I don't know why we would do that. So we gathered data on enemy, military facilities, not on civilian facilities. And that's what I forwarded to my superior. So there's no point in distinguishing between a civilian and a military. So there would be only data, information, on military facilities, on military equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Again, you might not be able to assist us by telling us, but did your department have any responsibilities for reporting or gathering intelligence on locations where artillery rounds impacted? To put it a different way: Did your department have responsibility to gather information on the effects of artillery fire in the city?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is undoubtedly very profound, but from which side are we talking about? Are we talking on the Serb side or on the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did understand in the city to be on the BiH side. But if I'm wrong, that's a reference often used I think by both parties. So the question is whether your service ever had any responsibility to gather information on the effects of artillery fire that landed and fell on the opposite part of the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that was not within the remit of the intelligence service. That was quite superfluous.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'd like to say this, but I was only interpreted at half. If we can watch this, and if we can pay attention.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Perhaps the counsel could wait until interpretation finishes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for the Serb booth, I did not say that it might not be unimportant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's totally unclear what you're talking about at this very moment, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Could you please explain yourself, because I do see that you said you were only interpreted at half. Is that in the English interpretation or in any of the other languages?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. President, in order not to waste time, perhaps the English booth can do the necessary clarifications in the evening, and everything will be clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's the booth who works on it. But I do understand that drew our attention to a linguistic problem. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say if any department had responsibility for monitoring this; and if so, which?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean on our side?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a department did not exist. But I simply don't see a way, even if it did exist, I don't see a way that such a department could carry out such a task because, of course, it was about the other side that we're talking about. But certainly such a department did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But isn't that precisely what your department was about, to gather information about the events occurring on the other side?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Again, I have to clarify. For the umpteenth time, the essence of the intelligence department and its purpose, all the data on the enemy which points to the degree of our forces being at risk, this was interesting for our -- for my section, for my department in a sense that we were trying to prevent suffering a surprise at any kind of different line. Everything else was unnecessary. It was superfluous, except the data which was referring to the degree of risk that our forces were exposed to. That was what my commanders were interested in. And other data, information, is completely irrelevant. We were not interested in the other information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You are saying that yourself and your commander are not interested in the effects of artillery fire in a city with a substantial civilian population? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. Still, no, no, absolutely not. Because it was strictly observed that the actual, real targets are hit. I believe that you are trying here to twist my answer here. That doesn't mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... The question. I mean, you are entitled to say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that does not stand as such, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is now 10 minutes before the break. And the matter that I would want to go into are matters which I would only go depending on some inquiries. As I indicated to the Court, the time that might be used would be quite substantially shortened if we were allowed to proceed tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, perhaps we could go into private session and listen to, if we can hear some of these measures and inquire as to what is to be done and what could not be done beforehand. Perhaps we could be told the reason why the Prosecution needs this extra time. We did not have very accelerated rhythm, so I don't see why now the Prosecution has to be given this extra time to take other measures and reposition its troops. We were never allowed to do this, and we do not see why the Prosecution would be given leave to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, would you be willing to give further explanation in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't think it requires private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it be done in the presence of the witness or should we first ask the witness to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If the witness could be asked to leave, that would be more convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are discussing at this moment whether we will continue right away with your testimony or as the Prosecutor has asked we would continue at a later moment. Is there as far as you are concerned, is there any booking already made for your return, or is there any time restraint as far as you are concerned? I do understand that you perhaps would like to go back as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. There are no limits, no restrictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I don't know whether we'll see you back today or only tomorrow. May I nevertheless instruct you already in case we would not see you back, that you would not discuss with anyone the testimony in this Court. Thank you very much. Would you please follow, then, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are trying to locate some documents, the contents of which we would like to ask the witness about. And those contents relate to certain matters which are involved in some of the documents that were put to him. Secondly, the witness made reference to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you, is that documents put to him, you are talking about these reports or?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Secondly, although we were given summaries, the summaries were very general, and the witness did refer to certain matters in very precise fashion, matters involving the airport, matters involving a certain person who was said to have been disciplined, a brigade commander. And although in a general sense, the summaries would have covered some of these things, we would like to make some particular inquiries before we put certain things to the witness. I could, if time would permit to check the record, there were one or two others which arose. As I indicated, perhaps upon inquiry, we might not even need to ask him some of these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you're talking about saving a considerable amount of time, what is in your mind approximately, Mr. Stamp? Let's say in the best-case scenario.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the best-case scenario, saving an hour to an hour and a half, a whole session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp -- Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is there anything you'd like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. Mr. President, what I wanted to find in what the Prosecution said, the smaller element whatsoever, but I just found a tiny portion of information, but nothing more significant, and I believe that we can -- have to call a spade a spade, and I believe the Prosecution is asking for extra time. There's only one element that has been revealed, and perhaps that would be surprising -- not surprising to the Prosecution, because what it seems to come out from the transcript of the interview which took place between the Prosecution representatives and the Lieutenant-Colonel Indjic, perhaps it's something to do with the very recent document, very recently communicated to us, and it's perhaps it's to do with that that the Prosecution is worrying about surprising elements. Now, as to this witness, this is a soldier, a military officer. We always said we would ask officers to testify. And it is obvious that this is somebody who can testify on these matters. I don't think that the Prosecution -- there's no reason why they should stop and then continue the cross-examination later. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although some of the reference you made are not familiar to me, at least, for example interviews. I'm not aware of that. But apart from that, Mr. Stamp, the Chamber would prefer the cross-examination to take place uninterruptedly. That means that until now, since the Defence raised the issue that you're trying to find extra time, the Chamber will not grant extra time. Up until now, the Defence took four hours and 15 minutes. The Prosecution has taken up until now, if my bookkeeping is correct, approximately 1 hour and 25 minutes. So you'll not be granted more time as usual as the Defence. So therefore, we would like you to continue the cross-examination after the break of this witness, and you'll not get extra time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll adjourn until 5 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, you may proceed once the witness has been brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bukva, we are continuing at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Bukva, did you ever receive any information at any time that civilians sometimes crossed the airport runway?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know if any of the members of the staff at Lukavica were in receipt of any information of that nature, and that is that civilians sometimes used the runway?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that no one received such information, and I repeat, by a political decision taken by the authorities of Republika Srpska, the airport was handed over to the UN forces to be used only for humanitarian purposes. The French Battalion that was located at the airport was responsible for cases of abuse of the airport. But in any event, people did cross over the runway, and this was illegal. But a minute ago, I think that I explained that they were under the control -- it was under the total control of BH army units. It was either accidental, it was intentional, but the positions were by the airport runway itself. So no one could have passed by the combat disposition of those units. They couldn't have crossed over the runway without the local Muslim commanders being aware of the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is it because no one could have crossed the runway without the BH commanders being aware of the fact why you have concluded that no civilians crossed the runway?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This question has already been answered when the witness answered about intercepted telecommunications of the enemy army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that would not exclude such a thing, but you may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to repeat what the Defence has just reminded us of. By monitoring enemy communications, their radio links above all, we knew what was at stake, what was happening with regard to these -- the crossing of the runway. If there was a local commander -- one local commander in Butmir and one in Dobrinja and they were speaking to each other, and one of them said this evening I'll send you a hundred parcels, we were well aware of the fact that this meant a hundred soldiers. Why would local commanders discuss a hundred civilians crossing the runway? What would they need civilians for? Isn't it obvious that soldiers are concerned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These are conclusions, Mr. Bukva. The question is whether you know that civilians ever crossed, whether they were mentioned in communications or not, whether it would be wise to do so, whether it would be useful to do so. Did civilians ever cross according to your knowledge? If you have no knowledge, tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, civilians didn't cross the runway. And our soldiers used cunning. For example, if they saw a large group crossing the airport area, it was very easy for them to identify them by firing a burst of fire into the air. Then usually they would receive a reply. Fire would be returned. And this would immediately mean that the people in question were soldiers. Have you understood me in have I been clear enough?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So one way would be to open fire --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said in that last answer that usually fire would be returned. And I understand from that that there were occasions when fire was not returned. In those situations, could you conclude that these were civilians crossing the runway?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Look, just a minute, please. At times visibility was poor, you understand. It's a well-known fact that there is often thick fog in Sarajevo, and especially in the airport area. It's possible that an observer at the front line noticed something happening. But that there were no men, there were no groups. In case, there weren't any men either, but that is to say the other side did not return fire. But that doesn't mean that there were or there weren't any people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your answer. Could I just ask again, you spoke of your soldiers using cunning, and that they would fire a burst. And usually, there was return fire. And I think that you were saying that from that, you could conclude that those persons were not civilians. What I'm asking you is this: When those persons crossing the airport did not return fire, could it be concluded that these persons might be civilians?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object. I object with regard to the scope of the last question -- the last answer that the witness provided, and in particular with regard to the presence of or lack of such presence of people there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I also have some difficulties, Mr. Stamp. Did I understand your last answer to be that if you couldn't see because of the fog that someone was crossing, that you sometimes would fire anyhow, and that you could draw no conclusions if no fire was returned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I was clear. If the fighters at the front line, if they weren't sure that they had observed people on the runway, in such cases, they wouldn't open fire in order to "identify" people on the runway. When visibility was poor, this was almost impossible. And under cover of the fog, the Muslim forces could get large groups of soldiers in via the airport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but it's still a bit unclear to me. Because what you say, "if because of the fog you couldn't see whether there was someone on the runway," that you would not open fire. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that does not explain why there sometimes was no return fire, because you would expect return fire only if there was any previous firing. So if you did not fire when there was fog, you couldn't see it, the question then is what would explain the absence of returned fire when that happened? Mr. Piletta-Zanin, unless there's any technical issue like translation --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's perhaps a matter of translation because I think that what the witness said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may indicate the page and the line where you think there might have been a mistranslation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't spoken about mistranslations yet, but I will verify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said where you think there might be -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quite right. Yes, Mr. President. I think I heard this more clearly in a different language. But no, I won't say anything. But I think that the position that the witness expressed can be negatively deducted, inferred, from what he said at line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't want you to comment, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. You may refer to whatever page and line, and then we will ask the witness again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's exactly what I am doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. You said: "I think that the position that the witness expressed can be..." I invited you to state the page and line.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's page 63, line 9 and 10. And I won't think about anything any more. In particular, at the end, the last four words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I will read part of a previous answer, as it has been translated to us in English. And I would like you to confirm or to deny that it is what you said. You said: "In case there weren't any men either, but that is to say the other side did not return fire. But that doesn't mean that there were or there weren't any people there." Is that what you said? I'm not asking for further comment, but I'm just trying to find out whether this is what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you explained to us about the fog and the difficulties of seeing whether there was anyone there or not on the runway. And then I asked you that if you would not have opened fire because of bad visibility, and perhaps not being sure that there was anyone in the fog, that if you did not fire, what would under these circumstances explain the absence of return fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there is no return fire, that doesn't mean that civilians are in question. Similarly, it doesn't mean that there is someone on the runway. I think that's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Might be no one. Might be civilian. Might be military. Might be a grandmother. Might be a general. It could be -- so do I understand your answer to be that if there was no return fire, which is a bit of an odd expression, if there was no fire opened at all, that you could not draw conclusions as to the absence of any fire whether returned or at all? You wouldn't know whether there wasn't someone there; neither would you know if there would have been someone there what kind of person it would have been.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] More or less, that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You spoke to us of a commander of the Igman Brigade, one Mr. Dunjic. Did you at any time become aware of a situation or an allegation that this Commander Dunjic or this officer, Dunjic, assaulted the accused general?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assaulted in what sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: By physically striking a blow. And all I'm asking you simply is whether you did or did not become aware of an allegation or a situation that this occurred.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there was a conflictual situation, but in relation to this event, I don't know about it. I couldn't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As an intelligence officer, did you ever get an opportunity to have a look at that United Nations Monitoring Officer situation report?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you read or speak English?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is the cross-examination. May it please, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, is there any need to re-examine the witness, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. First of all, the Defence would like to have the audiocassette in the Serbian language; and in particular, as far as page 63, line 9 and 10 in the transcript is concerned. And this is the page that we have spoken about. We would like to have this. There is a question that I would like to ask, but that's on the basis of what I was able to hear and we might have a technical problem in this case. I'm not sure if we can do this now or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid not at this spot; the tape is still running, isn't it? Usually during the break, if any access is needed, we could try to locate it and you could ask questions to the witness about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you in advance for your help, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the apostacy that you mentioned to us, was this a historical reality?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're to trust historical records, yes, it's true. If you want me to provide a more detailed explanation --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. To treat someone as an apostate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I withdrew the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: To treat someone as an apostate, as in the expression Julian the Apostate, is that something that is negative to, describe someone in this manner?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, listen. In this specific case, it's a historical fact. What I said is a historical fact. So someone who has converted to the Islam faith has more or less become a Turk.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, very well. But that wasn't my question. My question was if one says that someone did something in historical terms, is this negative in your opinion, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to go back to the issue of Hrasnica. We spoke to you about the shelling -- you were spoken to about the shelling of refugees. You started answering the question, but you didn't carry on. You said that there weren't refugees there. I would like you to say why there were no refugees there.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it's a well-known fact that part of the town called Hrasnica, even before the war, was inhabited by Muslim people almost exclusively. And I don't see a reason -- maybe someone has other information here. But I don't see why refugees should be a term used in relation to that geographical area. As far as I know, there were no refugee camps there. Therefore, it is quite certain that it's part of the town which even before the war was inhabited almost exclusively by Muslims. I couldn't mention an exact percentage, but I'm very familiar with the situation in Sarajevo. I have been there since 1981. And I can claim this with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Was the army present there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that we will need the assistance of a technician because unfortunately, the computer didn't resist my manipulations, my manoeuvres. Thank you very much. Could Madam Registrar perhaps aid me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you spoke about a certain number of meetings that you attended at the level of the main staff. Thank you. Could you just say whether you also participated, attended these meetings, when the General and if the General was not there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think there were a few occasions when I did attend such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. It was just a matter that I wanted to clarify. At page 83 and afterwards, you spoke at length about the media in response to questions from the Prosecution. And in particular, you spoke about manipulations or rather about propaganda. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. To the extent that you mentioned propaganda, could you tell us what the purpose of this propaganda was?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Please, could you tell us what the purpose of this propaganda was, but before doing so, can you mention two or three cases are clear examples of such propaganda if you are able to do so?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Objection. Although the expression propaganda was used, in what was in fact not a responsive manner to the question I asked, the area that Defence counsel is entering into does not arise in re-examination. There was no issue as to the purposes of propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- your question was about taking advantage, your question was"do you recall saying that the Sarajevo Romanija Corps was taken advantage of in the media," which comes close to what I understand because it was in answer to that question that the witness referred to. Then you asked whether this would include reports in the media that members of Sarajevo Romanija Corps shelled civilians and shot at civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, but respectfully, I would submit that that first question was really bringing the witness's mind to something he had said something before in chief. Do you recall that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but I would not --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would allow the Defence to ask this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... You first asked for three examples which is a very factual question. So could you please first give clear examples of what you meant that was propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with your leave, my question was also to find out if the witness knew with which purpose, with which objective, was this propaganda organised? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's exactly the reason why I asked him first to perhaps answer the second question, because you did put two questions to him. Then we at least have the start with the facts, and then perhaps the answer to your first question might become more clear. Would you first tell us, give us some examples of propaganda.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As it happens, it was recently that I had the opportunity to see on -- in the media the testimony of the commander of the special sniper unit called Seve. This special sniper unit and this commander said that a French soldier in the area of the engineering school at Marin Dvor was killed by a sniper --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you. Are you now referring to television recording of a testimony in this Court? It's not quite clear to me. You say I had the opportunity to see in the media the testimony of the commander of the special sniper unit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't express myself well. It's not testimony before this Court. In relation to this incident that I'm talking about, the Serb side was accused of committing in the media when it happened. Furthermore before General Galic came, we had the incident at Vasa Miskin Street for which, after a while, it turned was not caused by the Serb side but the information, as it came out, went around the world. Furthermore, on our side at least, it is stated vehemently that the Markale incident was not caused by the Serb artillery or by the Serb mortar. When expert analysis, this was confirmed by Colonel Demorenko who was at the time chief of staff of UNPROFOR in Sarajevo as an expert for artillery. But again, this event went around the world, and it had the effect that it did have now. If you'll allow me, I can explain with what purpose all this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: So all of these activities were calculated with the objective of showing that part of town under Muslim control to the attention of the world as a victim. That is, being tortured, so to speak, by some uncivilised people from around the mountains that are going down on to the city and fighting the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm now referring to page 44, and the following. The Prosecution asked you if you have ever found out or if you learned that the shelling, the illicit shelling, had taken place on civilians targets, whatever they were. And you started to answer and said that was never the case. You were interrupted by the Prosecution, which is their right. But now, I would like you to elaborate on this. Why, when shells may have landed in the city of Sarajevo, why are you stating that this was never the case? Why are you saying that never have the Serb forces shelled, or at least not voluntarily, willingly, why have the Serb forces never shelled civilian targets? Could you answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before we -- may I just be -- the Court's kind indulgence, could the passage which is referred to be read to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is your computer ready again or not? Otherwise, I would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my paragraph is perhaps not the correct one. But it is somewhere on page 44 where the witness said, and I quote the end of his sentence: "... Events did not exist." And then we have a cabalistic sign where it says that the testimony has not been revealed to the public. I don't know whether my learned colleague Stamp has managed to find the paragraph I'm referring to. And I'm referring to line 12. This is coming after a Prosecution question referring to shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will read the part you are referring to. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, your line you just quoted, "but such events did not exist" is page 44, line 12. Would that be -- I would like you to be relatively precise, because at least I did not hear, but I might be wrong in my recollection, that on page 73, you introduced on line 4 a few words that in my recollection was rather an interpretation of the testimony than a reflection of the testimony itself. So therefore I would invite you to quote as precisely as possible the testimony you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please. Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. Mr. President, do you want me to quote the entire answer given by the witness? The witness answered the following to a question that was in reference to shelling of civilian: "That's false, absolutely false to say that that happened, but I don't specifically remember saying or seeing that in the media that there was such information, but such events did not exist." And then there is the sign that I mentioned earlier. Should I quote on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whenever it's needed for putting it to the witness, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, to a question of the Prosecution in reference to the shelling of civilians, and the way that was broadcast in the media, you said that this was false, and that these events never took place. Now, first of all, what do you mean by "these events"? What do you mean by that? Do you mean about the broadcasting or do you mean the shelling, just to be perfectly clear?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My claim is, first of all, in relation to what was said to the declaration that civilians had been shelled. This did not happen. But I also said that I do not recall that I had seen such an information in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now that you explain that you told me that such shellings by your army had never taken place, that the city under the control of the BH army was not shelled, can you please give me some more information regarding this.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question. I believe that there is something wrong with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Since you say that this is false, since the Serb army never shelled part of the city that remained under the control of the BH army, could you please elaborate on this.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm stating, I'm saying, that there was no shelling of civilians as this could be heard here. But that the artillery fire was opened exclusively on military targets. And we have spoken a great deal about those.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, now I'd like us to go back to the videotape in memory. Do you still have those images in your mind?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you remember that you identified the contours, silhouette of a church?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is the following: To the extent that this -- the way that this was filmed, this was filmed on ground level, do you have the same view from the top floors of your office and from the windows of the office of General Galic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's logical that the view would not be the same. The ground-level view, filming, was done from the immediate vicinity, or perhaps from the area of the line of trees. Naturally, from that area, the view is much clearer than from the windows of my office or of the commander, of General Galic. And then another thing - I don't remember whether we've mentioned it or not - in the area located between the area of the soldiers' club and the corps command, somewhere halfway, because of the enemy Browning activity from the area of Dobrinja and Donja Kotorac, in order to protect the commander and his offices, we erected steel slabs which completely obstructed the view because they protected from the bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Just to say, I presume that these slabs were just added temporarily because you could not see them on the tape.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, they could not be seen on the tape. The filming was done after the war, in the post-war period, and there's no reason for them to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to finish with this witness so he doesn't have to come back. But I don't know whether the Chamber has other questions. Perhaps I'll have three or four questions yet to go for tomorrow. It's just a question of organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Bench will have some questions for the witness. So perhaps it will be then better to -- then if this is a suitable moment for you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, to adjourn, how much time would you approximately need tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll have three or four questions, Mr. President. So very few things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll adjourn until tomorrow- I wanted to say in the morning, but it's in the afternoon as you all know by now. I would like to -- let me just confirm. One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The parties should be aware that it's not for the full hundred per cent sure that we'll be in the same courtroom, but we'll be sitting on from quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. We'll adjourn until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there is just one observation to make.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel put his microphone on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I am just being reminded that the following witness will be DP2, and I believe that there are just measures, protective measures, in his case for the new people who are here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then I've got another question for you,

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You asked for the tape, the audiotape. Could you indicate what audiotape you'd like to have, the live tape or the B/C/S tape or -- I don't know whether you want to check the original language or the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will need the B/C/S, that is, the Serbian language, so that I can check what has exactly been said, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did write that down. And through the registry, I'll inform you how you can get knowledge of the tape. We'll adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00 in this courtroom or Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: at 1.46 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 29th day of January, 2003, at 2.15 p.m.
